content:
Quick answer: On 10 October 2026, published UK guide prices for a private primary hip or knee replacement ranged from about £12,750 to £17,000, with a first consultant appointment from around £200 and tests often extra. Prices change, so get a written quote. Check free NHS options first, such as your right to choose in England, and remember you keep your NHS entitlement if you pay privately.

Prices checked on 10 October 2026 on the published self-pay pages of Circle Health Group and Nuffield Health, alongside Department of Health and Social Care guidance on NHS patients who pay for additional private care and BMA guidance on private care and general practice. Prices change often and vary by hospital, consultant and your health. We have no commercial relationship with any provider and the prices below are examples, not recommendations.

When an NHS wait is long and arthritis is affecting your sleep, work or independence, paying for private treatment can feel like the only option. Before you commit any money, it helps to know what is usually included, what costs extra, how private care fits with your NHS care, and whether there are free routes you have not yet used. This guide sets out the facts so you can make a calm, informed decision.

Before you pay: check the free options first

  • Your right to choose (England). If you are referred for a first outpatient appointment with a consultant-led service, you can usually choose any provider offering that service to the NHS, which can include independent hospitals that treat NHS patients. The care is still NHS-funded. Ask your GP which providers are available and compare waiting times. Our guide to how NHS referrals work explains this.
  • Asking to move provider. In England, if you are likely to wait longer than 18 weeks for consultant-led treatment, you can ask to be offered an alternative provider. Contact the hospital or your local integrated care board.
  • Self-referral physiotherapy. Many areas let you refer yourself to NHS MSK physiotherapy, which is free and often a core treatment for osteoarthritis.
  • Clinical review. If your symptoms have worsened, tell your GP or the hospital team. Your priority on the list may change.
  • Interim support. See our waiting list guide for what you can do while you wait.

Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland do not have the same legal right to choose a provider as England. Ask your GP or health board what options exist locally.

Published self-pay prices (checked 10 October 2026)

Large hospital groups publish guide prices online. The figures below are taken directly from their own pages on the date shown. They are starting or guide prices only, and the final price is confirmed after you have seen a consultant.

TreatmentPublished guide pricesWhat the provider says is included or excluded
Primary hip replacementFrom around £12,750 (Circle Health Group); average guide price £16,579 (Nuffield Health)Circle: fixed-price package covers surgery and appropriate aftercare; initial consultation and pre-surgery tests charged separately. Nuffield: treatment price includes pre-assessment, surgery and post-discharge care; initial consultation from £200 on top.
Total knee replacementFrom around £13,020 (Circle Health Group); average guide price £16,914 (Nuffield Health)As above for each provider.
Knee arthroscopyFrom around £4,276 (Circle Health Group)Guide price for self-pay patients. NICE says not to offer arthroscopic lavage or debridement to people with osteoarthritis, so ask why it is being suggested.
Initial consultant consultationAverage from around £200 (Circle Health Group); from £200 (Nuffield Health)Varies by consultant and hospital; tests during the appointment are extra.
PhysiotherapyInitial appointment from £101, follow-ups from £76 (Circle Health Group); initial assessment £72 outside London or £79 in London, follow-ups £49 or £52 (Nuffield Health)Price per session. The total depends on how many sessions you need.

Taken together, these published examples put a private primary hip or knee replacement roughly in the range of £12,750 to £17,000 before any extras, and a first consultant appointment from around £200. Other providers, regions and individual consultants can be cheaper or more expensive. Prices change, so always get a written quote.

We have not quoted prices for MRI scans, X-rays, injections or private rheumatology care because we could not verify current national published prices from a named provider on the day we checked. These prices vary widely by location and by which body part is being scanned. Ask any provider for a written price before booking.

What affects the cost

  • The hospital and region. London prices are often higher, as the physiotherapy example above shows.
  • The consultant. Consultant and anaesthetist fees can be included in a package or billed separately.
  • Your health. Other conditions, such as heart or lung problems, diabetes or a higher body weight, can mean extra tests, a longer stay or a higher-care bed.
  • The type of procedure and implant. Complex or revision surgery and some implants cost more.
  • Diagnostics. X-rays, scans and blood tests before treatment are often charged separately.
  • Length of stay and aftercare. Check how many nights, physiotherapy sessions and follow-up appointments are included.
  • Complications. Ask what happens, and who pays, if you need extra treatment or readmission.

Questions to ask before you agree a price

  1. Is this a fixed, all-inclusive price? What exactly does it include?
  2. Are consultant, anaesthetist and hospital fees all included?
  3. Which tests, scans and appointments are extra, and how much do they cost?
  4. How many nights in hospital and how many physiotherapy sessions are covered?
  5. How many follow-up appointments are included, and for how long?
  6. What happens if there is a complication, or I need to come back in?
  7. Does the hospital have on-site critical care, or would I be transferred to an NHS hospital if I became very unwell?
  8. What is the cancellation policy, and can I get a refund?
  9. How many of these operations does the surgeon do each year?

Get the answers in writing. Our list of questions to ask your consultant covers the clinical side.

How private care fits with your NHS care

Department of Health and Social Care guidance for England says NHS patients can pay for additional private care while keeping their NHS care, but the two must be kept as clearly separate as possible. In practice:

  • You do not lose your NHS entitlement because you pay for private care. You can go back to NHS care, which is based on clinical need.
  • Tell the NHS hospital if you have had your treatment privately, so they can remove you from the waiting list. If you only had a private consultation, ask whether you should stay on the NHS list.
  • You usually cannot mix NHS and private elements in one episode of treatment, such as paying privately for part of the same operation.
  • Private consultants can refer you to NHS services if you would be eligible for an NHS referral, according to the BMA. You are then treated according to clinical need, not jumped up the list.

Health is devolved, so Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have their own policies, but the same broad principle of separating NHS and private care applies. Ask your GP or health board if you are unsure.

Private prescriptions and ongoing medicines

This matters most for inflammatory arthritis. If a private rheumatologist starts a medicine, you may assume your GP will take over. That is not automatic. The BMA says a GP should only prescribe if they agree with the advice and feel able to prescribe safely, and it advises against shared care arrangements with private providers because of the principle of keeping NHS and private care separate. If your GP declines, prescribing and monitoring stay with the private provider and you pay for them.

Disease-modifying medicines such as methotrexate need regular monitoring blood tests, and biologic medicines are specialist-prescribed and expensive. For most people with suspected inflammatory arthritis, an urgent NHS rheumatology referral is the safer long-term route. Ask your GP whether your referral is urgent; NICE says suspected persistent synovitis should be referred urgently.

If you are thinking of a private joint replacement

  • Check the surgeon. All doctors must be registered with the General Medical Council, and you can check the GMC register online. Ask how often they do the operation.
  • Check the hospital. Independent hospitals are inspected by the Care Quality Commission (England), Healthcare Improvement Scotland, Healthcare Inspectorate Wales, or the Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority (Northern Ireland). Reports are published online.
  • Ask about rehabilitation. Physiotherapy after surgery is essential. Check how much is included and where it happens.
  • Plan for recovery costs. You may need help at home, equipment, transport and time off work.
  • Prepare as you would for NHS surgery. Our guide to preparing for joint replacement applies either way.

Private hospitals may not offer the same on-site support as a large NHS hospital, such as intensive care. Ask what would happen if you became seriously unwell.

Private scans

Private MRI and X-ray are widely available, and some providers accept self-referral. Before paying, check whether you need a scan at all. NICE says osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed without imaging, and scans often show changes that are common at any age and may not explain your symptoms. A scan report without a clinician to interpret it can cause worry rather than answers. See our guide to MRI scans and arthritis.

If you do have a private scan, ask for the images and report to be sent to your GP and NHS team. They may still choose to repeat it under NHS protocols.

Private medical insurance

  • Check if you already have cover. Some employers provide private medical insurance as a benefit. Ask HR.
  • Read the exclusions. Many UK policies exclude pre-existing conditions and ongoing chronic conditions, which can include arthritis. Some cover acute flare-ups or new problems. Check the exact policy wording before relying on it.
  • Get pre-authorisation. Insurers usually require approval before treatment, and may need a GP referral.
  • Check excesses and limits, including outpatient limits that may not cover scans or physiotherapy.

We do not recommend any insurer or product. If you have a complaint about an insurer that you cannot resolve, the Financial Ombudsman Service is free.

Paying and borrowing

Several providers offer monthly payment plans or medical loans, sometimes interest-free over a short term. A loan is still debt. Check the total cost, the interest rate after any interest-free period, and what happens if you cannot keep up. For free, impartial money guidance, contact MoneyHelper or a debt advice charity such as StepChange or Citizens Advice before you borrow.

Some people use savings, family help or crowdfunding. Think carefully about what you would do if further treatment, a complication or ongoing medicines were needed.

Treatment abroad

If you are considering surgery abroad, think about follow-up care, flying soon after surgery, legal protections and what happens if something goes wrong once you are home. Speak to your GP before booking.

Making the decision

A simple way to weigh it up:

  1. Write down your expected NHS wait, using official waiting time sources for your hospital.
  2. Write down what the wait is costing you: sleep, work, income, independence, mood.
  3. Get two or three written quotes and compare exactly what is included.
  4. Consider the long-term costs, especially ongoing medicines and monitoring.
  5. Talk it through with your GP and someone you trust before signing anything.

There is no right answer for everyone. Paying privately is a personal choice, and staying on the NHS list is just as valid.

When to get medical help

Do not delay urgent care while you compare prices. Get help the same day from your GP or NHS 111 if you have a hot, swollen, very painful joint, especially with a fever, or if you take an immune-suppressing medicine and develop a fever, sore throat or signs of infection. Call 999 or go to A&E if you have back pain with numbness around your bottom or genitals, or loss of bladder or bowel control, chest pain, or severe breathlessness. After any operation, NHS or private, seek urgent help for a hot, red, swollen or leaking wound, a painful swollen calf or sudden breathlessness.

Frequently asked questions

How much does a private hip replacement cost in the UK?

On 10 October 2026, Circle Health Group published a starting price from around £12,750 for a primary hip replacement and Nuffield Health an average guide price of £16,579, with an initial consultation from about £200 on top. Prices change and depend on the hospital, consultant and your health, so get a written quote.

Will I lose my NHS place if I see a private consultant?

Not automatically. Government guidance says you keep your NHS entitlement. If you go on to have your treatment privately, tell the NHS hospital so they can update the list.

Can my GP prescribe a medicine a private consultant recommends?

Sometimes. The BMA says GPs should only prescribe if they agree and feel able to do so safely, and shared care with private providers is not recommended. If your GP declines, the private provider stays responsible, and you pay.

Does private health insurance cover arthritis?

Often not for long-term care. Many policies exclude pre-existing and chronic conditions. Check your policy wording or ask your insurer directly.

If I am treated at a private hospital on the NHS, do I pay?

No. In England, independent hospitals can provide NHS-funded care, and you can often choose them at referral at no cost to you.

Do I need a GP referral for private treatment?

Not always. Some providers accept self-referral, but some consultants and most insurers require a GP referral.

What if something goes wrong after private surgery?

Contact the private hospital first, as many packages include aftercare. In an emergency, call 999 or go to A&E, as you are still entitled to NHS emergency care.
